To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

bivalve death and fossil assemblages in fine-grained, soft-sediment, siliciclastic subtidal environments in Bocas del TORO (Panama) contain a high diversity of encrusters and boring species, but a low diversity of damaged shells.
the preservation of bivalves in siliciclastic substrates is superb, and that the best preserved shells are in the finest-grained sediments.

(1) the quality of shell interior preservation in fine-grain siliciclasts is excellent; (2) the quality of preservation is poorer in mixed carbonate-siliciclastic and pure carbonate sediments; and (3) the quality of interior preservation is related to the presence of hard substrata, which provide a habitat for encrusters and bioeroders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the taphonomic signature of a major, but previously neglected, component of the tropical marine realm.

the taphonomic signatures and environmental controls on shell preservation in shallow subtidal environments of the Tropics and with the implications of these findings for interpreting the fossil record of tropical bivalve assemblages.
the taphonomy of bivalves from tropical siliciclasties and mixed siliciclatic-carbonate sedi-ments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the taphonomy of tropical siliciclasts is very good, but not as good as that of tropical carbonates.

taphonomic signatures in tropical siliciclasts are distinct from those in associated reefs and alga-dominated environments, but that they are not uniform across the full range of tropical sedimentary environments.
the taphonomic signature of a bivalve death-assemblage in a tropical fine-grained, soft-sediment environment is one of superb preservation and a low level of postmortem damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the best-preserved bivalve death-assemblages in the tropics are in siliciclastically dominated environments, and the most severely damaged assemblages are in mixed carbonate-siliciclastic environments.

the best-preserved bivalve death assemblies in tropical mixed silicticlastic-carbonatic settings are found in fine-grained, soft-sediment environments, where the best preservation occurs on the most protected and sheltered sites.
The main takeaway from our work is that

taphonomic variation in tropical siliciclasts and mixed siliclastic-carbonates is at least as large as that in tropical reefs and algal sand, and that taphonomic studies in these settings are as important as in reefs for understanding the taphonomic processes that shape the fossil record.
, contrary to the geological stereotype, fine-grained siliceous sediments are not necessarily taphonomically poor, but may be taphonomically excellent.
